books.section: Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, B. European Romanticism and American Culture

stimulus.text: Washington Irving's "Rip Van Winkle" (1819) tells of a Dutch settler in the Catskill Mountains who drinks with strange men, falls asleep for twenty years, and wakes to find his village changed: the portrait of King George III has become one of George Washington, and his neighbors argue about the new republic. Irving first invented the fictional historian Diedrich Knickerbocker in 1809 to tell a whimsical history of old New Amsterdam.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.9 B: Irving's humorous short stories, "Rip Van Winkle" (1819) and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow" (1820), portrayed a fanciful version of America, and in an 1809 novel he invented the fictional historian Diedrich Knickerbocker. Original synthesis, not a quotation.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Irving's story most clearly shows the influence of romanticism in which of the following?

options.text: Playful fantasy, fond of an imagined simpler past
Its careful statistics about trade and population
options.misconception: The village changes over twenty years, so it is easy to expect numbers about that change.

options.text: Its argument that the Revolution was a mistake
options.misconception: Rip is confused by the new republic, so it is easy to read his confusion as Irving's verdict.

options.text: Its call for Americans to copy British writers
options.misconception: Irving was popular in Britain, so it is easy to think he told Americans to copy Britain.

rationales.A: A man sleeping twenty years and waking to a changed world is fantasy with a backward, affectionate glance.
rationales.B: The story gives no trade figures or census numbers; its evidence is a tale, not a table.
rationales.C: Rip's confusion is a joke, not an argument; Irving celebrates the new republic's energy even as he laughs at it.
rationales.D: Irving's American stories were the point; he showed Americans could write their own tales, not copy Britain's.
rationales.general:
1. Name the strange part. A twenty-year sleep, strange men in the mountains, a village transformed overnight.
2. Match it to romanticism. Feeling, fantasy, and a fond backward glance are the movement's marks.
Background from the books: romanticism prized emotion and an imagined past over cold routine.
Remember: when a story runs on wonder instead of facts, ask which feeling it is built to give you.
